nodes.summary: The text estimates the labor burdens and costs for broker-dealers to identify potential conflicts and establish Regulation Best Interest training. Conflict evaluation would require 28,570 aggregate hours with no additional ongoing costs. Developing a computerized training module would cost approximately $21,600 per broker-dealer, or $61.7 million in total, plus 11,428 hours for compliance and legal approval. Initial representative training would require 435,071 hours, producing a total initial training burden of 446,699 hours. Annual repeat training would require another 435,071 hours per year.

nodes.title: (2) Ongoing Costs and Burdens
nodes.summary: The text estimates the initial and ongoing burdens of implementing Regulation Best Interest training. Broker-dealers would incur 11,428 hours to review and approve the training module, 435,071 hours to train registered representatives initially, and 446,699 hours in total, averaging 152.3 initial hours per broker-dealer. Requiring the one-hour training annually would create 435,071 burden hours per year, or 152.3 hours per broker-dealer, based on 435,071 representatives and 2,857 broker-dealers.

nodes.title: 2. Disclosure Obligation
nodes.summary: The proposed Disclosure Obligation would require broker-dealers to provide retail customers, before or at the time of a securities recommendation, written disclosures describing the relationship’s material scope and terms and all material conflicts of interest. The disclosures are intended to clarify account features, fees, services, and limitations, distinguish broker-dealers from investment advisers and dual-registrants, increase awareness of conflicts, and promote best-interest recommendations. The text also notes that related information-collection, record-making, and recordkeeping requirements will be discussed, and introduces a subsection explaining how broker-dealers are assumed to satisfy the relationship-disclosure requirement, although the excerpt ends before the methods are identified.

nodes.title: a. Obligation to Reasonably Disclose to the Retail Customer, in Writing, the Material Facts Relating to the Scope and Terms of the Relationship with the Retail Customer
nodes.summary: The text explains proposed Regulation Best Interest’s written disclosure obligations: broker-dealers must disclose material relationship terms and conflicts of interest before or when recommending securities to retail customers. These disclosures are intended to clarify accounts, fees, services, service limitations, provider roles, and conflict effects, thereby supporting best-interest recommendations. For compliance, broker-dealers are expected to use Relationship Summaries, standardized account disclosures addressing capacity and service scope, and comprehensive fee schedules, while also meeting related information-collection and recordkeeping requirements. Standalone firms may use the Relationship Summary to disclose capacity; dual registrants would use account disclosures explaining when they act as broker-dealers and how capacity changes will be communicated.

nodes.title: (1) Disclosure of Capacity
nodes.summary: The text explains proposed disclosure practices for broker-dealers, including using the Relationship Summary to disclose capacity for standalone firms, standardized account disclosures for dually registered firms, and comprehensive fee schedules detailing transaction, holding, and account fees and charges. These disclosures would generally be provided at the start of the customer relationship, with account disclosures also explaining capacity changes.

nodes.title: (2) Disclosure of Fees, Charges, and Types/Scope of Services
nodes.summary: The text explains proposed Regulation Best Interest disclosure practices concerning broker-dealer capacity, fees and charges, service types and scope, and material conflicts of interest. Capacity and service information would generally be included in standardized account disclosures delivered at relationship initiation, with updates for material changes. Comprehensive fee schedules would cover transactions, holdings, and accounts and would be updated when disclosures are no longer current or complete for a recommendation. Material conflicts would be disclosed in standardized written documents, supplemented with product-specific information, delivered at account opening or, for existing customers, before or when a recommendation is made, with further disclosures when circumstances materially change or additional information is needed.

nodes.title: b. Obligation to Reasonably Disclose in Writing All Material Conflicts of Interest that are Associated with the Recommendation
nodes.summary: The text explains disclosure requirements and estimated compliance burdens under Regulation Best Interest. Broker-dealers must update fee schedules when fee disclosures become incomplete or outdated, amend account disclosures after material service changes, and reasonably disclose all material recommendation-related conflicts in writing. Disclosures are generally provided at account opening, with existing customers receiving conflict disclosures before or at the time of a recommendation and additional updates as needed. The analysis assumes standardized and supplemental product disclosures, use of Relationship Summaries for capacity by standalone firms, new account disclosures for dual-registrants and service information, delivery for each customer account, and no separate representative-level burden for these disclosures. Conflict-identification costs are treated separately.

nodes.title: c. Estimated Costs and Burdens
nodes.summary: The passage introduces estimated annual reporting costs and burdens for Regulation Best Interest disclosures concerning broker-dealer capacity and the type and scope of services. It explains that standalone broker-dealers would use the Relationship Summary for capacity disclosure, while the analysis assumes dual-registrants would create new capacity disclosures and all broker-dealers would create service-related account disclosures, even if similar disclosures are already provided as a best practice. Disclosures are assumed to be delivered for each retail customer account. The Commission does not expect registered representatives generally to bear separate burdens because the broker-dealer’s account disclosure would cover the information, although the text begins an unfinished discussion of initial burdens for dually registered representatives. Conflict-identification costs are addressed separately under the Conflict of Interest Obligation.

nodes.title: (1) Disclosure of Capacity, Type and Scope of Services
nodes.summary: The text estimates the initial compliance burdens and costs for capacity, service-type, and service-scope disclosures under Regulation Best Interest. It assumes broker-dealers will provide standardized account disclosures for each retail account, with entities handling most disclosure responsibilities and dually registered representatives bearing capacity-related burdens. Each of 360 dually registered firms would spend 10 internal hours and $4,720 on outside counsel, producing aggregate initial estimates of 3,600 hours and $1.7 million. Material-conflict disclosure costs are covered separately.

nodes.title: i. Initial Burdens and Costs
nodes.summary: The text estimates the initial labor and external legal costs of creating standardized account disclosures on capacity and service scope for dual registrants, small broker-dealers, and large broker-dealers, as well as the labor required to deliver those disclosures to approximately 95.2 million retail accounts. It gives firm-level and aggregate hours and costs, explains the calculation assumptions and delivery timing, notes that postage costs are not incremental, and reports total initial burdens of 1,956,620 hours and costs of $20.04 million, with a minor discrepancy between the large-firm burden used in the total and the earlier estimate. Ongoing obligations are assumed to involve annual in-house review and amendment of the disclosures without outside-counsel costs.

nodes.title: ii. Ongoing Burdens
nodes.summary: The text estimates initial and ongoing burdens and costs for broker-dealers to prepare, update, and deliver retail account disclosures concerning their capacity and the types and scope of services offered. Initial delivery requires 1,956,620 hours and costs $20.04 million, with no incremental postage expected. Annual review, amendment, and delivery of updated disclosures are estimated at 427,700 hours, broken down by firm type and delivery activity. The Commission acknowledges that burdens vary by broker-dealer and introduces a standardized fee-schedule disclosure assumption for fees and charges.

nodes.title: (2) Disclosure of Fees
nodes.summary: The text estimates the ongoing burdens of updating broker-dealer account disclosures for changes in capacity and service scope, including 41,100 hours for large firms, 380,800 hours to deliver amendments to 20% of retail accounts, and 427,700 hours overall across firm categories. It notes that burdens vary by firms' products and services. It then outlines fee-disclosure requirements based on standardized fee schedules provided at relationship inception or before recommendations and amended for material changes, treating the burden as an entity-level responsibility. Initial preparation is estimated at five internal hours for small broker-dealers and ten for large ones, plus one-time outside counsel costs of $2,360 and $4,720, respectively; the excerpt ends before stating the aggregate initial burden.

nodes.title: i. Initial Costs/Burdens
nodes.summary: The text estimates the initial and ongoing burdens and costs for broker-dealers to create, review, update, and deliver fee schedules under Regulation Best Interest. It distinguishes small and large firms, quantifies internal hours and outside counsel costs for initial creation, estimates first-year customer-delivery burdens, and provides aggregate totals of 405,360 initial hours and $11.59 million. Annual updates are expected to require 1,604 hours for small firms and 8,220 for large firms, with no external update costs. Amendments after material changes would be delivered to an estimated 40% of retail accounts, although the excerpt does not state the resulting burden.

nodes.title: ii. Ongoing Costs/Burdens
nodes.summary: The text estimates broker-dealers’ initial and recurring burdens and costs for maintaining and delivering standardized fee schedules, including annual review assumptions, firm-size-specific hours, the absence of expected external costs, and the substantial burden associated with delivering amendments after material changes. It notes that these burdens may vary by firm because fee schedules differ. It then describes Regulation Best Interest’s requirement to disclose material conflicts of interest, assumes broker-dealer entities will handle disclosures for their representatives, and anticipates that firms will generally use standardized conflict-disclosure documents delivered at relationship inception for new customers and before or when recommendations are made for existing customers.

nodes.title: (3) Disclosure of Material Conflicts of Interest
nodes.summary: The text estimates the annual burden of updating standardized fee schedules and notes that costs vary by broker-dealer. It then describes Regulation Best Interest’s requirement that broker-dealers disclose all material conflicts related to recommendations, including the initial and ongoing burdens for entities and representatives. For analysis purposes, broker-dealer entities are assumed to make disclosures for their representatives, likely using standardized documents delivered at account inception for new customers and before or when recommendations are made for existing customers. The cited burden estimate is calculated from the number of affected retail accounts, time per disclosure, and number of broker-dealers.

nodes.title: i. Initial Costs and Burdens
nodes.summary: The text estimates the compliance burdens and costs associated with standardized fee schedules and Regulation Best Interest’s material-conflict disclosure requirement. It provides initial counsel, delivery, and aggregate burden and cost estimates for small and large broker-dealers, assumes standardized annual disclosures delivered at specified customer relationship or recommendation milestones, acknowledges alternatives such as as-needed or layered disclosure, requests comment on those alternatives, and introduces ongoing annual updating obligations without specifying mandated disclosure intervals.

nodes.title: ii. Ongoing Costs and Burdens
nodes.summary: The text estimates the initial and ongoing burdens and costs of creating, updating, and delivering standardized conflict disclosures under Regulation Best Interest. It provides broker-dealer and customer-account calculations for initial delivery, assumes annual in-house updates despite the rule's as-needed disclosure approach, and estimates recurring delivery burdens without outside professional costs. It also describes the Care Obligation and introduces related record-making and recordkeeping requirements intended to support compliance supervision, examinations, and investigations, including the requirement to record information collected from and provided to retail customers.

nodes.title: 3. Care Obligation
nodes.summary: The text estimates an annual ongoing burden of 761,600 hours, or 267 hours per broker-dealer, based on updating disclosures for a portion of retail accounts, with fee and conflict disclosures updated more often than service-related disclosures. It describes the proposed Regulation Best Interest Care Obligation, requiring reasonable efforts to assess recommendation risks, rewards, and potential customer benefit, while noting that its PRA burdens are covered under proposed Rule 17a-3(a)(25). It also introduces record-making and recordkeeping requirements under proposed Rules 17a-3(a)(25) and 17a-4(e)(5), intended to support internal supervision, compliance, examinations, and investigations, including a requirement to record information exchanged with retail customers.

nodes.title: 4. Record-making and Recordkeeping Obligations
nodes.summary: The text estimates disclosure-related burdens under Regulation Best Interest, explains the Care Obligation, and details proposed record-making and recordkeeping requirements. Broker-dealers would generally rely on existing customer records and systems but would need to document the associated person responsible for each relevant account, initially amend account disclosures, and enter this information for customer accounts. The estimated initial burdens include $378,544 for small firms, 4,110 hours for larger firms, and 3,808,000 hours for account-level data entry, with no expected ongoing burden for representative identification. Records such as Relationship Summaries, account disclosures, fee schedules, and conflict disclosures would generally have to be retained for at least six years, consistent with existing Rule 17a-4 practices.

nodes.title: b. Recordkeeping Obligations
nodes.summary: The text explains proposed broker-dealer recordkeeping and retention obligations under Regulation Best Interest and amendments to Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4. It identifies the records to be retained for at least six years, expects firms to rely on existing systems, estimates initial and annual burdens of approximately 15.9 million and 3.17 million hours respectively, discusses assumed and potentially additional storage and compliance costs, states that the information collections are mandatory, and addresses confidentiality by noting that customer written disclosures would not be confidential.

nodes.title: C.Collection of Information is Mandatory
nodes.summary: The text describes the estimated ongoing recordkeeping burden and costs of proposed amendments to Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, including a projected 3.17 million annual burden hours and no expected change in retention-compliance costs. It seeks comments on record-update frequency and possible additional retention costs, states that the specified information collections are mandatory for broker-dealers, and explains that Regulation Best Interest written customer disclosures would not be confidential. The burden estimate is calculated from expected annual updates to specified records across 95.2 million retail accounts at two minutes per document.

nodes.title: D.Confidentiality
nodes.summary: The text estimates a 3.17 million-hour annual ongoing recordkeeping burden under the proposed Rule 17a-4(e)(5) amendment, expects no increase in retention-compliance costs compared with current Rule 17a-4 costs, and seeks comment on record-update frequency and potential additional retention costs. It states that the related Regulation Best Interest, Rule 17a-3, and Rule 17a-4 information collections are mandatory for broker-dealers, that required written retail-customer disclosures are not confidential, and explains the burden estimate through projected document updates across 95.2 million accounts.

The section evaluates the training, disclosure, care, and recordkeeping requirements proposed under Regulation Best Interest. It quantifies the initial and recurring labor and dollar costs of developing and delivering training; preparing, updating, and distributing disclosures about broker-dealer capacity, services, fees, charges, and material conflicts; and maintaining related records. It explains the use of Relationship Summaries, standardized account disclosures, fee schedules, and conflict documents for standalone firms, dual registrants, new customers, and existing customers. It also describes the Care Obligation to assess recommendation risks, rewards, and customer benefit, together with record-making and six-year retention requirements designed to support supervision and regulatory examinations. Finally, it addresses mandatory information collections, confidentiality, existing systems, uncertain storage costs, and requests for comment on disclosure timing, updating frequency, alternative disclosure methods, and retention burdens.

nodes.title: D. Confidentiality
nodes.summary: The text estimates 3.17 million annual burden hours for ongoing recordkeeping under the proposed Rule 17a-4(e)(5) amendment and expects no change in retention-compliance costs, while seeking input on record-update frequency and possible additional costs. It states that the relevant information collections are mandatory for broker-dealers, distinguishes nonconfidential retail-customer disclosures from generally confidential examination and investigation submissions, and requests broad public comment on burden estimates, affected persons and firms, unidentified costs, and related issues. The comments will help evaluate the collections’ necessity and practical utility, estimate accuracy, and opportunities to improve the collected information.

nodes.title: E. Request for Comment
nodes.summary: The text addresses confidentiality of information provided during Commission examinations, requests public comment on the estimated reporting burdens and costs of Regulation Best Interest and related proposed recordkeeping amendments, and identifies specific estimates and collection issues on which feedback is sought under the Paperwork Reduction Act. It provides submission recipients, addresses, file references, and the 30-day timing recommendation for OMB comments. It then introduces SBREFA requirements, including the Commission’s obligation to advise OMB whether the proposal is a major rule, defined in part by an annual economic impact of $100 million or more.

structure.summary: The section analyzes the Paperwork Reduction Act implications of proposed Regulation Best Interest and related broker-dealer recordkeeping amendments. It identifies the affected broker-dealers and associated persons, explains the proposal’s disclosure, best-interest, conflict-mitigation, training, care, policy, and recordkeeping obligations, and estimates their labor, technology, training, and ongoing compliance burdens. It addresses mandatory collections, OMB review and control numbers, confidentiality, record retention, and examination information, while requesting detailed public comment on the estimates, practical utility, costs, disclosure and retention approaches, and possible omitted burdens. It also provides PRA submission information and introduces the proposal’s related SBREFA major-rule analysis, alongside questions seeking data on the economic analysis, customer and firm effects, market implications, and regulatory alternatives.

structure.title: VI. SMALL BUSINESS REGULATORY ENFORCEMENT FAIRNESS ACT
structure.summary: The text addresses reducing the burden of Regulation Best Interest information collections and provides procedures, mailing addresses, file references, and timing for submitting comments and requesting OMB materials. It then explains SBREFA's requirements for identifying major rules, including the economic, cost, competition, investment, and innovation thresholds, the potential 60-day Congressional-review delay, and the Commission's request for supporting comments on Regulation Best Interest and a proposed Rule 17a-4(e)(5) amendment. Finally, it introduces the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Act Analysis, describing the Commission's obligation to assess effects on small entities, citing the relevant statutes, and noting the Commission's authority to define small entities for its rulemaking.

structure.title: VII. INITIAL REGULATORY FLEXIBILITY ACT ANALYSIS

nodes.title: A. Reasons for and Objectives of the Proposed Action
nodes.summary: The text explains the RFA framework and presents the Commission's proposal for Regulation Best Interest. The proposal would require broker-dealers and associated persons making retail recommendations to put customers' interests first through disclosures, careful recommendations, and policies addressing ordinary and incentive-based conflicts. Its goals are to improve advice, reduce conflicts and investor confusion, harmonize regulation, align duties with expectations, and preserve affordable investment choices. It would also create specified record-making and six-year retention duties. The proposal is based on Dodd-Frank and several Exchange Act provisions, and it identifies small broker-dealers for RFA purposes using a $500,000 total-capital threshold.

nodes.title: B. Legal Basis
nodes.summary: The text describes proposed Regulation Best Interest-related record-making and six-year record-retention requirements for broker-dealers, including customer information and responsible associated-person identities. It states the statutory authority for the proposed rules and begins defining which broker-dealers qualify as small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act based on having less than $500,000 in total capital.

nodes.title: C. Small Entities Subject to the Proposed Rule
nodes.summary: The text explains that the proposed Regulation Best Interest amendments would impose new record-making and six-year record-retention duties on broker-dealers, identifies the statutory authority for the proposals, defines which broker-dealers qualify as small entities under the RFA, estimates that 2,857 retail broker-dealers—including about 802 small entities—would be affected, and introduces the required discussion of projected compliance obligations for small entities.

nodes.title: D. Projected Compliance Requirements of the Proposed Rule for Small Entities
1. Conflict of Interest Obligations
nodes.summary: The text addresses the small-entity impacts of proposed Regulation Best Interest and related amendments to Rules 17a-3(a)(25) and 17a-4(e)(5), including affected entities, required professional skills, and compliance costs. It focuses on Conflict of Interest Obligations requiring updated written policies and procedures, material-conflict identification, and compliance training. Initial implementation is expected to involve 40 hours of outside counsel work costing $18,880 per entity, or $15.1 million in total, plus 10 hours of in-house legal review per entity, totaling 8,020 hours, followed by ongoing costs and burdens.

nodes.title: a. Written Policies and Procedures
nodes.summary: The text outlines the estimated compliance costs and burdens for small entities under proposed Regulation Best Interest and related amendments to Rules 17a-3(a)(25) and 17a-4(e)(5). It focuses on conflict-of-interest obligations, including updating policies and procedures, identifying material conflicts, and developing compliance training. It provides estimated outside-counsel, consulting, programming, and internal staff costs and hours for initial and ongoing compliance, including aggregate totals for all affected small entities.

nodes.title: b. Identification of Material Conflicts of Interest
nodes.summary: The text estimates the costs and burdens for small entities under proposed Regulation Best Interest. Annual policy and procedure updates would cost about $3,850 per entity, or $3.08 million collectively, plus 4,010 internal hours. Identifying and assessing material conflicts would require technology modifications costing about $5,400 per entity and $4.33 million in total, along with 4,010 hours for coordination and another 4,010 hours to assess materiality. Ongoing annual conflict reviews would add 8,020 hours across 802 entities. The text then introduces training requirements under which small entities would develop programs to promote compliance and maintain and enforce written policies and procedures.

nodes.title: c. Training
nodes.summary: The text estimates the costs and labor burdens small entities would incur under proposed Regulation Best Interest for technology modifications and conflict-of-interest reviews, as well as compliance training. Technology changes would cost $4.33 million and require 4,010 hours, materiality determinations another 4,010 hours, and annual conflicts reviews 8,020 hours. Developing computerized training modules would cost $21,600 per entity, or $17.32 million in total, with 3,208 hours for management and legal approval. Initial and recurring annual training of registered representatives would each require 4,236 hours.

nodes.title: 2. Disclosure Obligations
nodes.summary: The text describes proposed Regulation Best Interest disclosure obligations for small entities: written disclosure of the relationship’s material terms, including capacity, fees, charges, service types and scope, and written disclosure of material recommendation-related conflicts. It then estimates that each dually registered small entity would require 10 internal hours and $4,720 in outside-counsel costs to prepare standardized capacity-disclosure language; across 41 entities with retail business, this totals 410 hours and $193,520. Footnotes provide the calculation, data and cross-references supporting these estimates.

nodes.title: a. Disclosure of Capacity, Type and Scope of Services
nodes.summary: The text explains the written disclosure and conflict-of-interest obligations proposed by Regulation Best Interest and estimates related burdens for small entities. It provides initial drafting, legal-review, delivery, and ongoing-update costs and hours for disclosures concerning capacity and service types and scope, including separate estimates for dually registered and standalone broker-dealers. It also estimates the initial internal and external costs of preparing fee schedules and begins estimating their delivery burden, based on 802 entities and approximately 7,845 retail accounts.

nodes.title: b. Disclosure of Fees
nodes.summary: The text estimates small-entity burdens and costs under Regulation Best Interest for disclosure delivery and fee schedules. It provides aggregate and per-entity hours for an initial disclosure, estimates fee-schedule creation at 4,010 hours and $1.89 million including outside counsel, calculates initial and amended delivery burdens using 7,845 accounts and 802 entities, projects 1,604 recurring annual update hours with no external update costs, and begins estimating counsel time for standardized material-conflict disclosures.

nodes.title: c. Disclosure of Material Conflicts of Interest
nodes.summary: The text estimates the paperwork burdens and costs for small entities associated with standardized fee schedules and material-conflict disclosures. Fee-schedule activities include an initial burden of 156.9 hours, annual updates totaling 1,604 hours, no expected external update costs, and 62.76 annual hours for delivering amendments to 40% of accounts. Conflict-disclosure development would require 4,010 initial burden hours and $1.89 million in aggregate external costs, with delivery to new and existing customers adding 156.9 initial hours. Annual updates would total 802 hours with no expected external costs, while delivery of amended disclosures to 40% of accounts would add 62.76 hours annually; per-entity burdens and calculation assumptions are provided throughout.

nodes.title: 3. Obligation to Exercise Reasonable Diligence, Care, Skill and Prudence
nodes.summary: The text states that small entities are not expected to incur additional costs from the reasonable diligence, care, skill, and prudence obligation. It then addresses proposed record-making and recordkeeping requirements under Rules 17a-3(a)(25) and 17a-4(e)(5), explaining that small entities already record relevant customer information and therefore would generally face no new record-making burden from information collection. However, they would have to record specified information for each retail customer receiving a securities recommendation, including the customer-related identities described in the incomplete text, while ensuring their analysis and recommendations meet Regulation Best Interest’s enhanced standard.

nodes.title: 4. Record-making and Recordkeeping Obligations
nodes.summary: The text addresses small entities’ obligations under Proposed Regulation Best Interest, concluding that the reasonable diligence, care, skill, and prudence obligation should not add costs or burdens or require additional customer information. It then discusses proposed record-making and recordkeeping amendments, explaining that existing records of customer investment profiles should prevent additional burdens for information collection, while noting a proposed requirement to record specified identities for each retail customer receiving a securities recommendation. The excerpt also references related discussions of costs, burdens, and monetized impacts and ends mid-requirement.

nodes.title: a. Record-making Obligations
nodes.summary: The text evaluates the costs and burdens for small entities under Regulation Best Interest. It concludes that the reasonable-diligence, care, skill, and prudence obligation should not create additional costs beyond existing information-collection practices. Proposed record-making requirements would require documenting the associated person responsible for each account, likely through amended account disclosure documents, at an estimated aggregate initial cost of $378,544 and 313.8 personnel hours, with no ongoing burden expected. Required records—including Relationship Summaries, account disclosures, fee schedules, and conflict disclosures—would be retained for six years using existing systems, requiring an estimated 1,307.5 initial hours but no anticipated uploading or filing costs.

nodes.title: b. Recordkeeping Obligations
nodes.summary: The text discusses record-making and recordkeeping burdens for small entities under proposed amendments to Rules 17a-3(a)(25) and 17a-4(e)(5). It identifies four records subject to six-year retention, estimates initial and annual burdens, explains that existing systems would be used and no significant costs are expected, provides the calculation assumptions and requests comment on them, and concludes that Regulation Best Interest would not conflict with and is generally consistent with the DOL Fiduciary Rule and related exemptions.

This section evaluates the projected reporting, disclosure, record-making, recordkeeping, and other compliance requirements and costs of proposed Regulation Best Interest and related amendments for approximately 802 small retail broker-dealers. It estimates the burdens of conflict-of-interest policies, material-conflict identification, technology changes, compliance training, relationship and fee disclosures, fee schedules, and conflict disclosures, including initial and recurring legal, consulting, technology, delivery, and staff costs. It also explains that the reasonable-care obligation is not expected to create material new costs, while proposed account documentation and six-year retention requirements would generally rely on existing systems, with limited initial record-making and recordkeeping burdens. The section includes calculation assumptions, aggregate and per-entity estimates, relevant professional-skill requirements, and a conclusion that the proposals are consistent with the DOL Fiduciary Rule and related exemptions.

nodes.title: E. Duplicative, Overlapping, or Conflicting Federal Rules
nodes.summary: The text estimates a 261.5-hour annual ongoing burden for small entities from the proposed Rule 17a-4(e)(5) amendment, with no expected increase over current Rule 17a-4 compliance costs. It addresses the RFA requirement to identify duplicative, overlapping, or conflicting federal rules, noting the DOL Fiduciary Rule and related BIC and Principal Transactions Exemptions, which are viewed as generally consistent with and not conflicting with Regulation Best Interest. The burden calculation and the agency’s requests for comment on record-update frequency and retention-related costs are also provided.

nodes.title: F. Significant Alternatives
1. Disclosure-only alternative
nodes.summary: The text evaluates three alternatives to proposed Regulation Best Interest: a disclosure-only regime, a flexible principles-based conduct standard, and fiduciary requirements modeled on the DOL’s BIC Exemption. It compares their compliance costs, flexibility, liability implications, and effectiveness in protecting retail customers, concluding that the first two would provide weaker protection and that the BIC-like approach could be costly despite potential savings for firms with existing infrastructure.

nodes.title: 3. Enhanced Standards Akin to BIC Exemption
nodes.summary: The Commission compares Regulation Best Interest with two alternatives: a less prescriptive principles-based standard, which could provide flexibility and lower compliance costs but might weaken retail protection, reduce clarity, and increase liability; and a fiduciary regime modeled on the DOL’s BIC Exemption, which could benefit firms with existing infrastructure but might raise advice costs, price customers out of the market, and impose significant burdens and market effects. It preliminarily favors the proposed approach, believes it may significantly affect many small entities, and requests comments and empirical data on those impacts and compliance burdens before introducing the statutory authority and proposed rule text section.

This section explains the RFA's required consideration of alternatives for reducing small-entity impacts, rejects exemptions, size-based requirements, and entity-specific simplification because they could weaken investor protection and regulatory consistency, but highlights flexible, performance-based compliance and disclosure options. It then compares disclosure-only, principles-based, fiduciary, and BIC-like alternatives in terms of protection, costs, flexibility, liability, clarity, and market effects, preliminarily favoring Regulation Best Interest while requesting data and comments on its impacts and burdens, particularly for small entities.

nodes.title: G. General Request for Comment
nodes.summary: The Commission explains that imposing a fiduciary standard and BIC-like requirements on broker-dealers could raise costs, reduce retail access to investment advice, affect the advice market, and conflict with its regulatory approach. It preliminarily concludes that Regulation Best Interest may significantly affect many small entities and solicits data-driven comments on affected entities, potential impacts, compliance burdens, and effects on smaller firms, followed by the statutory-authority section and related footnotes.

structure.summary: The Initial Regulatory Flexibility Act Analysis explains the RFA framework and legal authority for evaluating Regulation Best Interest and the proposed Rule 17a-4(e)(5) amendment, identifies approximately 802 affected small retail broker-dealers, and describes the proposals' investor-protection objectives, including customer-focused recommendations, disclosures, conflict management, and record retention. It estimates small-entity reporting, disclosure, technology, training, legal, consulting, record-making, and recordkeeping burdens; compares the proposals with existing DOL requirements; evaluates alternatives intended to reduce small-firm impacts; and preliminarily supports Regulation Best Interest while seeking comment on exemptions, flexible compliance, costs, burdens, and market effects. The Commission also requests empirical data concerning impacts on the economy, consumers, industries, competition, investment, innovation, advice access, and smaller firms, and notes the potential Congressional-review delay for major rules.

structure.title: VIII. STATUTORY AUTHORITY AND TEXT OF PROPOSED RULE
structure.summary: The Commission discusses the potential costs and market effects of imposing a fiduciary standard and BIC-like requirements on broker-dealers, including possible reduced access to advice for retail customers and disproportionate burdens on small entities. It seeks Regulatory Flexibility Act comments and supporting data on affected entities, impacts, and compliance burdens. The text then states the statutory authority for Regulation Best Interest and related recordkeeping amendments, identifies the affected CFR provisions and subject areas, and provides the continuing and newly added legal authority citations for proposed Part 240 rules.

structure.title: PART 240 – GENERAL RULES AND REGULATIONS, SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934
structure.summary: The text presents the SEC's 2018 proposed Regulation Best Interest under Dodd-Frank and the Exchange Act. It would require broker-dealers and associated persons making securities recommendations to retail customers to act in the customer's best interest through written conflict disclosures, reasonable care, and conflict-management policies; defines retail customers and investment profiles; and establishes related customer-record creation and six-year preservation requirements, along with the proposal's statutory authorities, subject classifications, and formal regulatory amendments.
